investment_summary:
Thermo Fisher's 2025 revenue rose 4% to $44.6 billion, but profit and cash lagged: EBITDA was flat, free cash flow fell 13% to $6.3 billion and total debt reached $39.4 billion [1][2][4]. Operating income still grew 6% to $7.75 billion, and EPS beat consensus in each of the last four quarters [1][3].

Consensus, dated after the 10-K, expects revenue growth of 7.7% in 2026 and 5.2% in 2027 [3]. The valuation asks for far more. At the current enterprise value of $290.4 billion, the reverse DCF needs 16.3% annual revenue growth for ten years, against a historical three-year CAGR of -0.3% [1][2][3]. On consensus growth the implied return is 5.3%, below the 9.1% discount rate, so the share price depends on a recovery the historical record does not yet show [3].

The main risks are leverage, $65 billion of acquisition goodwill and budget-driven demand from academic and government customers [1].
key_takeaways: Cash generation should recover as tax timing reverses, since free cash flow fell 13% to $6.34 billion in 2025 [1][2].
Analytical Instruments is the swing factor: its margin fell 3.2 points to 23.0%, so a recovery would lift group profit [1].
At the current enterprise value the stock needs 16.3% annual revenue growth, more than double consensus, so valuation risk outweighs near-term upside [2][3].
Leverage is the main risk: total debt rose to $39.4 billion, so coverage against the 3.5x covenant is the number to watch [1].
business_overview:
Thermo Fisher Scientific is a world leader in serving science, supplying instruments, consumables, reagents, diagnostics, laboratory products and outsourced pharma services. Revenue reached $44.56 billion in 2025, up 4% reported and 2% organically, with acquisitions and currency each adding about one point [1]. The company reports four segments: Laboratory Products and Biopharma Services ($23.98 billion, 14.0% segment margin), Life Sciences Solutions ($10.37 billion, 36.3%), Analytical Instruments ($7.55 billion, 23.0%) and Specialty Diagnostics ($4.68 billion, 26.9%) [1]. The company cites its PPI productivity system and a sales force of about 14,000 people as core advantages [1].

Portfolio changes have been central to growth. Olink, acquired in July 2024, added proteomics to genetic sciences, and the September 2025 acquisition of Solventum's filtration and separation business strengthened bioproduction [1]. Bioproduction grew $548 million on a reported basis, and genetic sciences added $82 million from Olink [1]. Restructuring charges of about $0.3 billion in 2025 are expected to yield annual savings of about $0.5 billion [1]. An agreement to acquire Clario Holdings was also announced, but its terms are not in the filing extract [1].

Capital allocation has shifted toward debt-funded growth. Total debt rose to $39.4 billion from $31.3 billion, as the company issued $8.85 billion of debt and paid $4.04 billion for acquisitions, while buybacks fell to $3.00 billion from $4.00 billion [1][2]. Cash and short-term investments reached $10.1 billion [2]. The stock closed at $512.27 at the filing date, a market capitalisation of $195.7 billion, within a 52-week range of $383.77 to $642.22 [2]. Consensus carries a Buy rating and a target price of $755.12, a view dated after the 10-K [3].
market_position:
Thermo Fisher sells into four end markets: pharma and biotech, academic and government, industrial and applied, and healthcare and diagnostics [1]. Sales grew in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific in 2025, while China declined [1]. The 10-K does not disclose market share, named customers or customer concentration, so its position must be judged from scale and segment growth [1]. On scale, 2025 revenue is about 1.8 times that of Danaher and 6.4 times that of Agilent, making Thermo Fisher the largest company in its peer set [4]. Scale brings procurement and distribution advantages, but it does not by itself guarantee share gains. Classification: Thermo Fisher is a scale leader in a budget-sensitive, technology-driven market rather than a share-taker.

Demand is uneven across customer types. Pharma services added $457 million and bioproduction added $548 million on a reported basis, while the research and safety channel added $422 million [1]. U.S. academic and government buyers showed hesitancy, and the federal government shutdown in October 2025 can delay budget-funded orders [1]. Instrument demand is also split by sector: chemical analysis fell $78 million, while electron microscopy grew $87 million [1]. COVID-19 vaccine and therapy activity moderated, weighing on the Laboratory Products and Biopharma Services segment [1].

Consensus expects revenue growth of 7.7% in 2026 and 5.2% in 2027, which requires the pharma and biotech channel to keep growing while academic demand stabilises [3]. Against peers, Thermo Fisher's 2025 revenue growth of 3.9% was ahead of Danaher's 2.9% but behind Agilent's 6.7% and IQVIA's 5.9% [4]. The market position is therefore strong on reach and scale but not clearly gaining share [1][4].
operating_results:
Revenue reached $44.56 billion in 2025, up 4% but still below 2022's $44.92 billion. Organic growth was 2%, with acquisitions and currency each adding one point [1]. Gross margin slipped to 40.9% from 41.3% as cost of revenue rose 4.5% to $26.32 billion, outpacing sales [1]. Even so, operating income grew 6% to $7.75 billion, and the GAAP operating margin improved to 17.4% from 17.1%, which the company attributes to productivity gains [1]. Cost discipline, rather than pricing or product mix, carried the year's operating profit growth.

Below operating income, net income rose 5.8% to $6.70 billion, helped by a GAAP tax rate of 7.5% against 9.3% in 2024 [1]. Net interest expense widened to $426 million from $312 million as debt rose [1]. Diluted EPS was $17.74 on a GAAP basis, up 7%, and $22.87 on an adjusted basis, up 5%, with 1.3% fewer diluted shares [1]. In our view the lower tax rate flattered EPS growth more than operations did, so the quality of the earnings gain is a point to watch. EBITDA was flat at about $11.5 billion, so the margin fell to 25.8% from 26.9% in 2024 [4].

Segment income was uneven. Life Sciences Solutions rose 8% to $3.77 billion, Laboratory Products and Biopharma Services rose 8% to $3.35 billion, and Specialty Diagnostics rose 8% to $1.26 billion [1]. Analytical Instruments fell 11% to $1.74 billion as its margin dropped 3.2 points to 23.0% on tariffs and mix [1]. Operating cash flow fell to $7.82 billion from $8.67 billion, and free cash flow fell 13% to $6.34 billion, mainly because $1.77 billion of working capital was used, largely from the timing of income tax payments [1][2]. Consensus expects FY2026 EPS of $25.28, with estimates raised over the past 90 days [3]; these consensus figures are dated after the 10-K.
risk_assessment:
The filing's three most consequential exposures are acquisition-related asset values, leverage and demand tied to customer and government budgets [1]. The first is goodwill and intangibles of about $65.2 billion, against total assets of $110.3 billion, or 59% of the balance sheet [1]. The value of these assets depends on the future cash flows of acquired businesses and on how well they are integrated, and an impairment would be a non-cash charge that reduces reported equity and earnings [1]. Tangible book value is negative at -$11.8 billion, so the balance sheet relies on intangible value holding up [1]. The filing also warns that acquisitions may be made at a premium and that expected synergies may not be realised [1].

The second exposure is leverage. Total debt rose to $39.4 billion from $31.3 billion, and total debt to equity reached 0.74 [1]. Net debt is $29.5 billion on the balance sheet [1]. The company must keep its net interest coverage at or above 3.5 times, measured on consolidated EBITDA, and a breach would be an event of default with cross-default effects [1]. The filing gives no EBITDA or interest expense figure, so the headroom cannot be measured from the document [1]. The $5.00 billion revolver supports liquidity, and cash plus short-term investments rose to $10.1 billion [1][2]. Refinancing costs are rising, however: net interest expense widened to $426 million from $312 million [1].

The third exposure is demand cyclicality. Some customers' spending depends on budget allocations, and the federal government entered a shutdown in October 2025 [1]. Order cancellations, delays and longer collection cycles are named as possible effects of weak economic conditions [1]. The filing also cites tariffs and foreign exchange as sources of margin pressure, which the Analytical Instruments segment showed in 2025 [1]. Against this, the customer base spans pharma, biotech, academic, healthcare and government buyers, which spreads demand across several funding sources [1].

The risks interact. Weaker customer spending would reduce earnings, tighten the coverage covenant and raise impairment exposure at the same time [1]. Consensus, dated after the 10-K, shows EPS estimates still rising, which lowers the near-term risk of a sharp earnings reset [3]. The stock's valuation, however, leaves little margin for error: the reverse DCF requires 16.3% annual growth against a historical three-year CAGR of -0.3% [2][3]. Trailing data show a Piotroski F-score of 5 of 9 and an Altman Z-score of 4.26, which suggests the company is financially sound but not without weak points [2].
competitors_analysis:
We selected Danaher (DHR), Agilent (A) and IQVIA (IQV) as peers. Danaher has the closest business model in bioprocessing, life sciences and diagnostics. Agilent overlaps most with Thermo Fisher's Analytical Instruments segment. IQVIA overlaps with its pharma services business. Revenue relative to Thermo Fisher is 0.5x, 0.2x and 0.4x respectively, and Thermo Fisher is the largest company of the four [4].

On growth, Thermo Fisher's 2025 revenue rose 3.9%, ahead of Danaher's 2.9% but behind Agilent's 6.7% and IQVIA's 5.9% [4]. Its gross margin of 40.9% is well below Danaher's 59.1% and Agilent's 52.4%, and above IQVIA's 33.3% [4]. Thermo Fisher's EBITDA margin of 25.8% is third of the four, behind Danaher's 28.3% and Agilent's 26.4%, and above IQVIA's 21.2% [4]. Its margin has been stable in a narrow band of 25.8% to 26.9%, but the gap to Danaher closed largely because Danaher's margin declined, not because Thermo Fisher improved [4].

Returns and cash conversion are weaker. Thermo Fisher's ROIC fell to 8.7% in 2025, the lowest in its series, against Agilent's 13.9%, IQVIA's 8.8% and Danaher's 5.4% [4]. Its free cash flow conversion of 0.94 is below IQVIA's 1.51 and Danaher's 1.46, and only Agilent's 0.88 is lower [4]. The tool's conversion ratio does not define its denominator, so this comparison should be read as indicative. Free cash flow fell 13.4% in 2025, the largest decline in the series [4].

On valuation, Thermo Fisher trades at an EV/EBITDA of 21.5x, the highest in its own four-year history [4]. Danaher is at 25.5x and Agilent at 23.4x, while IQVIA is much cheaper at 10.5x [4]. Thermo Fisher therefore trades below the two higher-quality peers on EV/EBITDA, even though its ROIC and cash conversion are weaker. The consensus view, dated after the 10-K, carries a forward EV/Sales of 6.0x for 2026 and a Buy rating with a target price of $755.12 [3]. Against the peer set, Thermo Fisher's scale and revenue growth are solid, but its returns and cash generation do not yet justify a premium to Agilent or Danaher [4].

investment_theses.evidence: Free cash flow fell 13% to $6.34 billion in 2025 as working capital used $1.77 billion [1][2]; trailing twelve-month free cash flow reached $7.60 billion at 2026-09-30 [2].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 10-K showing free cash flow above $7.0 billion (filed around February 2027) [1].
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2026 free cash flow below $6.3 billion, or operating cash flow below the $7.82 billion of 2025 [1].

investment_theses.thesis: Analytical Instruments margin recovers toward 26% as tariff and mix pressure eases, lifting group segment income.
investment_theses.evidence: Segment margin fell 3.2 points and segment income fell 11% to $1.74 billion on tariffs, mix and investment [1]; electron microscopy grew $87 million in 2025 [1].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 10-K showing Analytical Instruments segment margin at or above 25% (filed around February 2027) [1].
investment_theses.invalidation: Segment margin still below 23% in the FY2026 10-K, or a further tariff-driven margin decline [1].

investment_theses.thesis: Consensus revenue growth of 7.7% in 2026 is delivered and EPS estimates keep rising, but the current valuation needs far more growth than that.
investment_theses.evidence: Consensus EPS is $25.28 for 2026 and $27.77 for 2027; 23 analysts raised and 1 cut the current-year estimate in the last 30 days; the reverse DCF needs 16.3% a year [3]. EPS beat consensus in each of the last four quarters [3].
investment_theses.signpost: Q1 2027 results (around April 2027) showing revenue growth of at least 7% and an EPS beat versus consensus [3].
investment_theses.invalidation: Revenue growth below 5% in 2026, or a cut in the current-year EPS consensus below its current $25.28 level [3].

investment_theses.thesis: Leverage is manageable: debt-funded acquisitions and buybacks are supported by strong liquidity, but only if returns on capital recover above 9.5%.
investment_theses.evidence: Total debt $39.4 billion and net debt $29.3 billion [1][2]; current ratio 1.9x and Altman Z-score 4.26 [2]; ROIC fell to 8.7% in 2025 from 9.5% in 2024 [1][4]; total debt reached $41.4 billion at 2026-09-30 [2].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 10-K showing total debt at or below $39.4 billion and ROIC above 9.5% [1].
